Motivation & Emotional Processes

Motivation theories, emotions, stress and coping — how they affect patient behaviour and recovery.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe Maslow's hierarchy of needs
  • Define emotion and list basic emotions
  • Explain stress and coping styles

In simple words

Motivation is what drives behaviour toward a goal. Emotion is a feeling state such as fear, joy or anger. Stress is the body’s response to demands; coping is how a person manages it.

Nurses meet patients who are frightened, in pain or stressed — understanding motivation and emotion helps them care better.

Maslow’s hierarchy of needs

Level Need Example
1 Physiological Air, food, water, sleep
2 Safety Security, freedom from fear
3 Love and belonging Family, friends, relationships
4 Esteem Respect, achievement, confidence
5 Self-actualisation Reaching one’s potential

Lower needs must be mostly met before higher needs become urgent. A patient gasping for breath (physiological) cannot focus on self-esteem.

Emotions

Basic emotions include happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust. Emotions have three parts:

  • Physical changes (heart rate, hormones)
  • Behaviour (facial expression, action)
  • Feeling (how it is experienced)

Stress and coping

Stress is the body’s response to a threat or demand. The general adaptation syndrome (Selye) has three stages: alarm, resistance and exhaustion.

Coping styles:

  • Problem-focused — tackle the cause directly.
  • Emotion-focused — manage the feelings (talking, relaxation, prayer).

🔴 Maslow for nursing

Meet lower needs first. A patient who is short of breath, in pain or frightened needs physiological and safety care before teaching or esteem support.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Prioritise care — airway, breathing and circulation first (physiological), then safety.
  • Acknowledge emotion — name the feeling (“You seem worried”) and listen.
  • Reduce stress — explain procedures, give time, involve family, teach relaxation.
  • Motivate change — link advice to what matters to the patient (family, work, independence).
  • Watch for exhaustion — long stress leads to burnout in patients and staff; encourage rest and support.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Maslow’s hierarchy: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation.
  2. Lower needs take priority over higher needs.
  3. Basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust.
  4. Stress response stages (Selye): alarm, resistance, exhaustion.
  5. Coping: problem-focused (tackle cause) and emotion-focused (manage feelings).

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Motivation is what drives goal-directed behaviour.
  2. Intrinsic motivation comes from within; extrinsic from outside rewards.
  3. Emotions have physical, behavioural and feeling parts.
  4. Long-term stress can cause exhaustion and illness.

📌 Memory trick

Maslow’s levels bottom-up: “Pee Safe Love Esteem Self” — Physiological, Safety, Love, Esteem, Self-actualisation.

60-second revision

  • Motivation drives goal behaviour; emotion is a feeling state.
  • Maslow: physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, self-actualisation.
  • Lower needs first — ABCs and safety before teaching.
  • Stress stages: alarm, resistance, exhaustion.
  • Coping: problem-focused and emotion-focused.
  • Basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust.

Test yourself

Maslow's most basic need is:

Answer: C. Physiological needs (air, food, water) form the base of Maslow's pyramid.

Which need must be met before esteem?

Answer: B. Lower needs — physiological, safety and love/belonging — come before esteem.

The alarm stage of stress is part of:

Answer: B. Selye's general adaptation syndrome has alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages.

Problem-focused coping means:

Answer: B. Problem-focused coping deals directly with the source of stress.

A patient who is gasping for breath needs:

Answer: B. Physiological needs come first in Maslow's hierarchy — airway and breathing are priority.
